Module 4

DNA, Chromosomes & Replication

Every one of your body's cells carries the same full set of genetic instructions. This module covers where those instructions are stored, how they are packed into chromosomes, and how the cell makes a perfect copy of them before it divides.

2. DNA Structure, Nucleotides & Base-Pairing Rules

What makes species different? Every living organism uses the exact same four DNA bases. Diversity between individuals and species comes strictly from the sequence (order) of the nucleotides.

Nucleotide anatomy: every DNA nucleotide is a monomer built from three components, and it is the nitrogenous base that is the only part that changes from one nucleotide to another.

PHOSPHATE
GROUP PENTOSE
SUGAR NITROGENOUS
BASE

A nucleotide is made up of three components:

  • A phosphate group - contains phosphate.
  • A pentose sugar - a 5-carbon sugar.
  • A nitrogenous base - the only part that changes from one nucleotide to another.

The bonds: the two strands of the DNA double helix zip together down the middle using hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.

Chargaff's base-pairing rules

Adenine pairs with Thymine (A–T), and Guanine pairs with Cytosine (G–C).

"Apples in the Tree, Cars in the Garage"
A–T and G–C are the only legal pairs: the dashed lines are the hydrogen bonds zipping the two strands together.

3. DNA vs. RNA (Comparing Nucleic Acids)

DNA
double helix, two strands
RNA
single-stranded (most RNA)
FeatureDNARNA
StructureDouble helix (two strands)Single-stranded (most RNA)
Base PairingA–T and G–CA–U and G–C (no Thymine!)
Unique BaseContains Thymine (T)Contains Uracil (U) instead of Thymine
U stands where T stood.
If a strand shows A–U pairing, you are looking at RNA, never DNA.

4. Chromosomes & Karyotyping (Packing the DNA)

DNA is way too long to fit loosely in a cell, so the cell organizes it like thread on spools.

CENTROMERE
holds the two sister chromatids together
  • Chromosome: a complex of DNA and associated proteins carrying the cell's genetic information.
  • Histones: the protein spools that eukaryotic DNA wraps around to build chromosomes.
  • Sister chromatids & centromere: two identical copies of the same chromosome (sister chromatids) held together at the waist by a centromere.
  • Homologous chromosomes: matching pairs (one from mom, one from dad) that have the same length, shape, and genes.
  • Autosomes: non-sex chromosomes, chromosome pairs that are the same in males and females.
  • Chromosome number: most humans have 46 chromosomes total. A diploid cell has two sets of chromosomes, which is 2 times the chromosome number of a haploid cell.
Karyotype: an organized image of an individual's full complement of chromosomes.
  • Count total chromosomes to spot a missing chromosome or an extra copy (3 copies of chromosome 21 = Down Syndrome).
  • Check pair #23 to identify biological sex (XX = female, XY = male).

5. DNA Replication (Copying the Chart Before Shift Change)

When it happens: during the S (Synthesis) phase of the cell cycle.

The model: DNA replication is semiconservative: each new DNA double helix consists of one old (original) strand and one new strand.

original
double helix
replicate
copy 1
old + new
copy 2
old + new

The step order & key players

  1. Enzymes unwind and separate the two DNA strands.
  2. Primers (short, single strands of DNA or RNA) base-pair with the single DNA strands to create an attachment point.
  3. DNA polymerase attaches to the primer and adds complementary nucleotides to build the new strand.
The primer lands first, always.
DNA polymerase is the famous builder, but it cannot start a new strand on its own: no primer on the strand, no polymerase at work.
Module 5

Gene Expression & Mutations

Think of your cell as a busy hospital. DNA is the master medical chart locked safely inside the Nurse's Station (the nucleus), and it never leaves the room. To build proteins (the "meds and treatments" your body needs), the cell copies instructions onto a disposable sticky note (mRNA) and sends it out to the floor (ribosome).

1. Gene Expression Basics

  • Gene: a unit of information encoded in the sequence of nucleotide bases in DNA.
  • Gene expression: the multistep process of converting information from a gene into a functional RNA or protein product.
DNA
transcriptionRNA polymerase
mRNA
translationribosome + tRNA
Protein

2. Step 1: Transcription (DNA → mRNA)

The enzyme: RNA polymerase builds the mRNA strand in eukaryotes.

How to transcribe (practice): match the DNA template strand antiparallel (3′ → 5′ becomes 5′ → 3′) and swap every T for U in the RNA product:

DNA template
3′TGACAAGCT5′

mRNA product
5′ACUGUUCGA3′

3. Step 2: RNA Splicing (Editing the Rough Draft)

Before eukaryotic mRNA leaves the nucleus, it gets edited like a movie reel:

  • Introns: non-coding sections that are spliced (cut) out before translation.
  • Exons: coding sections that stay in the final mature mRNA and code for the final amino acid sequence.
"Ex"ons are "ex"pressed; "In"trons are "in"tervening trash.
Exons exit the nucleus to become protein. Introns get cut out and stay behind.

4. Step 3: Translation (mRNA → Protein)

  • Codon: a sequence of three nucleotides on mRNA that specifies an amino acid.
  • Anticodon: a complementary sequence of three nucleotides on tRNA that matches the mRNA codon.
  • tRNA (transfer RNA): the delivery truck that delivers amino acids to the ribosome during translation.
amino acid on top · anticodon on tRNA
mRNA codon below

The mRNA runs through the ribosome three bases at a time (codon). Each tRNA arrives carrying one amino acid, checks that its anticodon complements the codon, drops off its cargo, and leaves. Link by link, the protein chain grows.

5. Mutations (Charting Typos in DNA)

Definition: mutations are permanent changes in the DNA sequence of a chromosome.

  • UV light damage: exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light causes nucleotide dimers, which create a physical kink in the DNA double helix.
  • Exon mutations: because exons code for the final protein, a mutation inside an exon region changes the amino acid sequence of the resulting protein.
UV → nucleotide dimers
a physical kink in the helix
Permanent means permanent: a mutation is not a temporary or intermittent change; it sits in the DNA sequence until it is repaired or passed on.

Types of mutation

Mutation TypeWhat HappensExample
Base-pair
substitution		One base is swapped for anotherCCU-GAG… → CCU-GUG…
(A swapped for U; sickle cell)
InsertionOne or more nucleotides are added into DNAExtra base pushed into the sequence
DeletionOne or more nucleotides are removed from DNACystic fibrosis (most common fatal genetic disorder in the U.S., caused by a deletion) and a form of thalassemia (loss of the 20th nucleotide region of beta globin)

Practice Questions

  1. Chargaff Math: A sample of human DNA contains 22% Adenine. What percentage of the bases in this sample are Cytosine?
  2. DNA History: Which researchers used bacteriophages to prove that DNA, not protein, is the genetic material injected into bacteria?
  3. DNA Structure: Which chemical component makes one DNA nucleotide different from another, and what type of bond links complementary bases together across the double helix?
  4. Chromosome Anatomy: Two identical copies of the same replicated chromosome are called _______, and they are attached together at a constricted region called the _______.
  5. DNA Replication Order: In DNA replication, enzymes first unwind and separate the two strands of DNA. What exact step happens immediately next?
  6. Replication Model: Why is DNA replication described as semiconservative?
  7. Transcription Practice: Transcribe the following DNA template strand into its complementary mRNA strand (include the 5′ and 3′ ends):
    3′CATGGATCA5′
  8. RNA Splicing: During eukaryotic mRNA processing, which segments are spliced out, and which segments remain to code for the final amino acid sequence?
  9. Translation: Which specific type of RNA contains an anticodon and delivers amino acids to the ribosome?
  10. Mutations:
    Case A: A patient's beta-globin gene is missing a nucleotide, drastically altering the resulting protein. What type of mutation is this?
    Case B: Exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light creates a physical kink in the DNA double helix. What is this kinked structure called?
